headline: Ram Island bait balls hold tight, but the albies haven't found Stonington yet
subhead: Bass are stacking on structure as the tide rebuilds out of neap — the false albacore push is close, just not here.
body_markdown:
I poled the skiff over the boulder field off Wamphassuc Point on the last hour of Wednesday's ebb and watched a school of peanut bunker come apart against a rock the size of a Buick — scattering in every direction, some of them skipping clear of the water. That's the tell. Something was under them, working the seam where the current pinches between two granite heads about four feet down. I couldn't get a fly through it before the school reformed and slid off toward deeper water, but I didn't need to see the fish to know what that was. Bass do that to bait around here. Bluefish don't bother with the subtlety.

That's been the story most of this week — bait getting nervous around structure, current doing the work, fish showing up when the tide gives them a reason to. We flagged this last week — said the Sound's current had gone soft on the neap cycle and the bite would come back as the tide rebuilt — and that's exactly what's happening. New London is reading 69.4 degrees, which is comfortable water for stripers to sit tight to rock instead of running deep and nocturnal like they're doing out west where Kings Point is pushing near 71. That few degrees of difference matters. It's why Fishers Island Sound is still a daylight program right now while other parts of the coast have gone to bunker-and-eel-after-dark mode.

The stripers I'm finding are on the classic spots — the boulder chain running off Ram Island, the rock pile east of Wilcox Reef, and the drop just outside the Stonington breakwater where the bottom goes from six feet to eighteen in about thirty yards. Slack water and the first hour of the flood have been the window. I'm throwing a 3/8-ounce bucktail dressed with white curly-tail, working it slow along the bottom contour so it ticks off the rock without hanging. On the fly side, a olive-and-white Deceiver on an intermediate line, cast tight to the boulders and stripped erratic, has drawn some of the better fish — nothing huge, mostly 22 to 28 inches, with the occasional fish pushing 34 that made the leader hum for a few seconds before it wedged me into the rocks and I lost it. That's the tax you pay fishing this water. You lose gear here. It's part of the deal.

Fluke have been steady rather than spectacular, which is about right for this time of year. The mouth of the Mystic River and the flats off Enders Island are holding fish on the last of the outgoing, staging on the sand pockets between the mussel beds. Four-inch white Gulp on a bucktail, dragged slow, has been out-producing bigger baits — the fish down there are picking, not aggressive, and a subtle presentation gets more bites than a big splashy one. Keepers have been mixed with plenty of shorts, so it's a sort-through-them program, not a fill-the-cooler one. Black sea bass are doing what they always do out toward the Watch Hill Reef and around East Point — reliable, unglamorous, biting green crab and squid strips on the bottom in eighteen to twenty-five feet. If you want dinner and don't need a story to go with it, that's still the surest bet in this whole stretch of water.

Now, the albies. Everybody's asking, and I don't have them yet. The setup is close — the temperature threshold that gets albies moving has already been crossed out at Montauk, Block Island, and up into the Buzzards Bay corridor, and this section of the Sound is usually one of the earlier stops once that push starts working west, given how close we sit to those eastern approaches. But close isn't here. I ran Wicopesset Passage and along the edge of Fishers Island at first light three mornings this week looking for that nervous, scattered bait pattern that means albies are working underneath it, and what I found was gulls sitting quiet on the water and bait moving in slow, undisturbed pods. That's not an albie sign. That's just bait doing its thing.

What I'd watch for over the next week: the tide is building back out of neap toward the August 12 new moon, which means more current strength through Fishers Island Sound and Little Narragansett Bay, and that's exactly the kind of push that tends to bring the first scouting albies and bonito in behind the bait they're chasing. If I had one morning to spend chasing them, I'd be at the Watch Hill rip or working the rock line off Napatree Point on an outgoing tide with a small epoxy jig rigged and ready, because that's usually the first place this water shows sign — even a single blitz that lasts ten minutes and then vanishes. Until then, the stripers on structure are the honest play. Fish the rock, fish it slow, and respect that this ground doesn't give anything away for free. It never has, going back to when my grandfather was running boats out of the Portuguese fleet — you learn where the rocks are, or you pay for not knowing.
